source: Reality figures: HBAI (as above). Perception framing: Ipsos Perils of Perception; academic studies of income self-placement; ONS ASHE 2024 for individual pay.
note: The 'perception' side of this essay is mostly the reader's own live guess. External belief claims are kept qualitative where a precise, verified survey figure was not to hand.
self_placement: Study after study finds the same thing: asked to place themselves on the income ladder, people cluster near the middle, whether they are near the top or near the bottom. The rich feel typical; the poor feel typical.

beliefs.text: Almost everyone, rich or poor, guesses they sit somewhere near the middle. It is one of the most reliable findings in the study of how people see money.
beliefs.src: Ipsos Perils of Perception; income self-placement studies

beliefs.text: The real middle: median equivalised household income after housing costs is £562/week, about £29,250 a year for a couple with no children. Half of Britain lives on less.

People picture income as an individual salary. Full-time median pay is around £37,000 gross. But living standards are measured on net household income, shared across a household and adjusted for its size.
The average (mean) income is £694/week, but two in three households earn less than that. A long tail of high earners drags the average above the typical.
Pensioners are pictured as the face of hardship. After housing costs they now have the lowest poverty rate of any age group, because so many own their home outright.
Children have the highest poverty rate: roughly one in three lives below the line after housing costs, nearly double the pensioner rate.
